column1: rdap-whois|C|C1|crest|Why might an HTTPS RDAP result replace a traditional WHOIS response during registration research?|RDAP provides structured registration data through a different protocol|RDAP is an SSH credential-dumping command|WHOIS is the only possible source of registration data|RDAP automatically authorizes scans of every listed address|Registration data can be accessed through different interfaces. Record the source and available fields rather than equating a tool name with the whole task.|A data source's interface can evolve.

rir-domain|C|C1|crest|Why distinguish IP address registration from domain registration?|Their registries describe different resources and relationships|Both always identify the application's ultimate owner|An IP registry lists every database user|A domain registrar assigns every Ethernet MAC|Netblock and domain data can reveal related but distinct administrative information. Hosting and ultimate ownership need corroboration.|An infrastructure registry is not a full business ownership map.

netblock-scope|C|C1|crest|A registry returns a /16 allocation for a hosting provider. What should an assessor infer about testing scope?|The allocation is context, not permission to test every address|The whole /16 is automatically in scope|Every listed address runs the client's application|The registry grants administrator credentials|A public allocation can contain many unrelated tenants and services. Preserve the engagement's actual asset boundary.|Registration breadth does not expand authorization.

registry-stale|C|C1|crest|Why preserve the lookup date when using registration data?|Fields and associations can change over time|The date authenticates every response cryptographically|Every old record is necessarily false|A current date proves every listed system is live|Registration evidence is time-specific. Historical records can remain useful but must be labeled and corroborated.|Current attribution and historical attribution are different claims.

privacy-redaction|C|C1|crest|A domain's contact details are privacy-redacted. What remains a useful collection approach?|Use permitted public metadata and corroborating sources|Assume the domain cannot belong to the client|Guess a hidden personal contact as fact|Treat the privacy service as every application owner|Redaction limits fields, not necessarily all useful attribution. Avoid converting missing public data into an ownership conclusion.|Unknown is not the same as absent.

registry-referral|C|C1|crest|A WHOIS response refers to another registry. What can that indicate?|More relevant resource information may be held there|The target automatically permits a zone transfer|The response includes a valid administrator session|The client's scope covers every referred organization|Referral can improve collection completeness. It remains a source relationship rather than an access grant.|Follow data provenance without inheriting new scope.

contact-identity|C|C1|crest|A technical contact email appears in registration data. Why should it not automatically be treated as an active employee account?|It may be an alias, role mailbox, proxy, or historical contact|Every contact is the current domain administrator login|Every contact carries the site's password|Registration addresses always bypass mail authentication|Use the address as an attribution lead. Account existence, organizational relationship, and authority require separate evidence.|A public contact string is not an authenticated identity.

provider-correlation|C|C1|crest|Several domains share registrar and name-server providers. What is the strongest initial conclusion?|They share observed infrastructure associations|They necessarily share the same ultimate owner|They necessarily use the same passwords|They are all authorized target assets|Common services can be used by unrelated customers. Correlation should be corroborated, not promoted to ownership.|Shared infrastructure is often weak attribution evidence.

a-v-aaaa|C|C2|dnsbase|An A lookup has no data but an AAAA lookup succeeds. What does this show?|An IPv6 address record is available without that IPv4 record|The hostname necessarily does not exist|The domain has no authoritative servers|The application has no network exposure|Different record types can have different data. A negative answer for one type is not a universal name/service absence.|Query type limits the conclusion.

ptr-no-forward|C|C2|dnsbase|A PTR lookup returns a hostname. Why confirm forward resolution separately?|Reverse and forward zones are independently administered data|PTR guarantees a matching A/AAAA record|PTR is a validated login token|Reverse DNS lists every virtual host on the IP|Reverse naming can be stale, generic, or inconsistent. Forward checks can corroborate the relation without proving ownership.|A reverse name is not a complete identity assertion.

mx-priority|C|C2|dnsbase|MX preferences are 10 for primary and 50 for secondary. Which is conventionally preferred first?|The exchanger with preference 10|The exchanger with preference 50|The exchanger with the longer hostname|The exchanger with the larger IP address|Lower numerical MX preference is preferred. Equal values and reachability can affect selection.|Preference values are not a higher-is-better score.

mx-hostname|C|C2|dnsbase|An MX value names mail.example.test. What further information is normally needed to connect?|Address resolution for the named exchanger|The zone's SOA minimum as a password|The web server's HTTP Host header|The registrar's telephone extension|MX names a service host rather than directly carrying its transport address. Resolution and SMTP behavior are separate steps.|A routing record may require another lookup.

txt-spf-limit|C|C2|dnsbase|An SPF-style TXT record names an include provider. What can it reveal?|A dependency or policy association worth checking|Every user's exact mailbox password|Authorization to probe the provider's customers|A complete description of application hosting|Mail-policy data can disclose infrastructure dependencies. It does not prove every dependency is current or within scope.|A policy reference is a lead with its own context.

txt-arbitrary|C|C2|dnsbase|Why can TXT records disclose varied information beyond mail policy?|The record can carry administrator-defined text|TXT is restricted to one fixed authentication format|Every TXT value is encrypted by DNSSEC|TXT is an executable script on the browser|Applications use TXT for several purposes. Interpretation depends on format and issuer rather than the type alone.|Record type does not settle the meaning of every value.

cname-terminal|C|C2|dnsbase|app is a CNAME to service, and service has an A record. What resolution behavior is intended?|Follow the alias to its target's address data|Treat the alias text as a plaintext password|Replace the authoritative zone's SOA with app|Send every HTTP request to the resolver itself|CNAME expresses an alias; additional resolution finds the target data. Verify chains and actual service behavior separately.|Alias relationships are not direct application connections.

alias-chain-limit|C|C2|dnsbase|Why inspect the full CNAME chain rather than only its first target?|Later aliases can reveal the actual dependency and failure point|The first alias authenticates every subsequent host|Every alias guarantees a zone-transfer permission|Only the longest name can host a service|Several steps can change the final endpoint. Chain contents, freshness, and provider behavior all affect interpretation.|A first-hop dependency may not be the final dependency.

delegation-subdomain|C|C2|dnsbase|A subdomain has its own NS delegation. What does this imply for enumeration?|It may be served as a separate zone|Its records must all be in the parent AXFR|It necessarily has no A records|It must share the parent zone's serial|Delegation establishes an administrative boundary in the DNS namespace. Examine the relevant child authority within scope.|A domain subtree can contain several zones.

authoritative-recursive|C|C2|dnsbase|What is the principal distinction between an authoritative server and a recursive resolver?|Serving authoritative zone data versus resolving queries for clients|Using TCP versus always using UDP|Returning only IPv4 versus only IPv6|Having passwords versus having no passwords|A server may have both roles, but they are different functions and can be configured separately.|Role and transport are separate dimensions.

aa-flag|C|C2|dnsbase|What does the DNS AA flag relate to?|Whether the answer is authoritative for the queried name|Whether the caller is an administrator|Whether the response is encrypted|Whether a zone transfer was permitted|AA is an answer-authority indicator. It is not cryptographic authenticity or a user permission flag.|DNS header authority is not human authorization.

truncated-retry|C|C2|dnsbase|A UDP DNS response sets TC. What should the client consider?|Obtaining the full answer through an appropriate retry, often TCP|Treating the truncated bytes as the complete zone|Assuming every record is NXDOMAIN|Interpreting TC as the server's password policy|Truncation means the response is incomplete for that transport context. DNS clients commonly retry using TCP.|A partial response needs an explicit completeness check.

nxdomain-nodata|C|C2|dns|How does NXDOMAIN differ from NOERROR with no requested records?|NXDOMAIN denies the name; no-data can deny only that type|Both prove every service in the domain is absent|NXDOMAIN means the server accepted a zone transfer|No-data always means the client used the wrong password|Names and record sets are different DNS objects. Negative responses must be interpreted by status, type, and authority.|Name absence and type absence are different claims.

servfail|C|C2|dnsbase|A resolver returns SERVFAIL. What is a defensible interpretation?|The resolution operation failed; cause needs investigation|The domain necessarily does not exist|The website necessarily has no vulnerabilities|All records are intentionally public|Failure can reflect validation, upstream, configuration, or other conditions. It is not an NXDOMAIN-equivalent answer.|Resolution failure is not an existence answer.

refused-axfr|C|C2|dnsbase|A server refuses AXFR but answers ordinary records. What is established?|Transfer access is restricted on that tested path|Every record in the zone is secret|The server cannot serve authoritative DNS|All DNS enumeration techniques are blocked|Transfer restrictions are a specific control. Ordinary lookups, other nameservers, and public artifacts provide separate visibility.|One denied operation is not total nondisclosure.

zone-view|C|C2|dnsbase|Two authorized vantage points obtain different records for the same name. What should be considered?|Views, policy, caching, and response timing|A guarantee that one tool forged the data|A guarantee that both systems are different domains|A guarantee that DNS cannot use split views|DNS responses can legitimately differ by requester context or current data. Preserve each query's source and time.|Compare like-for-like observations before declaring contradiction.

ttl-countdown|C|C2|dnsbase|A cache stores a positive answer with TTL 600. After 200 seconds without refresh, what TTL is expected approximately?|400 seconds|600 seconds|800 seconds|2000 seconds|Remaining lifetime decreases with time. Requeries, replacement, and implementation policy can change the observed state.|A cached answer's TTL is remaining lifetime, not elapsed time.

soa-refresh|C|C2|dnsbase|Which SOA timer conventionally governs periodic secondary checks for updated zone data?|Refresh|Retry|Expire|Minimum|Refresh governs routine checking; retry concerns a failed refresh and expire limits serving without successful refresh.|SOA timers describe different maintenance events.

soa-retry|C|C2|dnsbase|A secondary's refresh attempt fails. Which SOA field conventionally informs the next retry interval?|Retry|Serial|RNAME|MNAME|Retry is the interval after failure. The serial tracks zone version and the name fields describe administrative information.|Failure recovery uses a different timer from normal refresh.

soa-expire|C|C2|dnsbase|Why is an SOA expire value relevant to a disconnected secondary?|It limits continued authoritative service without successful refresh|It determines every positive record's exact TTL|It controls the browser's cookie expiration|It is the zone administrator's password length|Expire is a zone-maintenance boundary. Record caching and application sessions use other lifecycles.|Do not reuse one timer's meaning across layers.

dnssec-confidential|C|C2|dnssec|What does DNSSEC not supply by itself?|Confidentiality of DNS query/answer content|Authentication of signed DNS data under valid trust|Integrity checking of signed record sets|Authenticated denial where correctly deployed|DNSSEC authenticates data; it does not encrypt ordinary DNS transport. Privacy mechanisms address another requirement.|Signing data and hiding data are different goals.

dnssec-signed-stale|C|C2|dnssec|Why can a validly signed DNS record still require operational interpretation?|A signature does not prove the named application is healthy or safe|Signing automatically verifies every site's authorization logic|A signed name necessarily uses HTTPS|A signature grants test permission to the caller|DNSSEC concerns DNS data authenticity and integrity. Service security and availability remain separate observations.|Authenticated naming is not application assurance.

ct-name|C|C1|crest|What can public certificate-transparency records contribute to reconnaissance?|Historical or current certificate-associated names|Every site's administrator password|A complete list of private database rows|Authorization to test all SAN entries|Certificate-associated names can reveal assets or history. Issuance time, ownership, and current resolution matter.|A name in a certificate is a lead, not current scope proof.

san-shared|C|C1|crest|A certificate lists several names. Why avoid assuming one name's approved scope covers all of them?|Certificate coverage and engagement ownership boundaries differ|SAN values are all automatically one application|Every SAN entry necessarily resolves to one IP|The certificate makes private addresses public|Names can belong to distinct services or contexts. Preserve the approved asset boundary while investigating relationships.|Cryptographic name coverage is not an engagement agreement.

archive-time|C|C3|crest|An archived page shows an endpoint absent from the current site. What should be recorded?|The endpoint's historical source and capture time|That it is currently reachable with identical behavior|That every historical secret is still valid|That the site's present owner approved testing it|Historical data can guide discovery but must be distinguished from current observations.|Past content is not automatically present behavior.

archive-secret|C|C3|crest|A historical public file contains a credential-like value. What remains to establish?|Its actual meaning, validity, scope, and consequence|That it grants current administrator access everywhere|That it is harmless because the archive is old|That every account in the organization shares it|A secret-looking artifact is a lead. Verify within authorization and avoid claims unsupported by the current state.|Credential appearance and usable authority are different facts.

robots-sitemap|C|C3|http|Why inspect both robots.txt and sitemap content?|They can reveal different discovery hints and URL sets|Both enforce resource authorization|Both prove every path exists now|Both enumerate every backend table|These publication mechanisms serve different crawler/navigation purposes. Confirm actual resource and access behavior.|Published URL lists are not access-control rules.

source-map|C|C3|crest|What can an exposed JavaScript source map add to review?|More readable source structure and original file references|Guaranteed server-side command execution|Every current user's plaintext password|The private key of every certificate issuer|Source maps can improve client-code visibility. Review disclosed content and actual backend boundaries separately.|Better source visibility is not automatic compromise.

bundle-endpoints|C|C3|crest|A bundle includes an endpoint string never reached during normal navigation. What is a useful next interpretation?|An unexamined functionality lead within the relevant scope|A guaranteed anonymous administrator endpoint|An automatic scope grant to all referenced hosts|Proof that the route executes SQL directly|Client code can reveal hidden workflow and obsolete routes. Confirm existence, state, and authority.|A string reference is not a validated live action.

public-backup|C|C3|crest|A backup file is indexed publicly but a current direct request returns 404. What should the result distinguish?|Historical publication from current retrieval behavior|A confirmed current unrestricted download|A guarantee that no copies exist elsewhere|A proof that the application has no backup process|Different sources and times can disagree legitimately. Preserve provenance and avoid conflating exposure states.|A current denial does not rewrite historical publication.

search-negative|C|C4|crest|A search engine returns no results for a company's internal host pattern. What can be concluded?|No matching indexed results were found with that query|No such hosts exist anywhere|The company has no internal network|All naming conventions are cryptographically secret|Indexing, syntax, freshness, and visibility limit search results. Alternative sources can provide other evidence.|A query's empty result has a coverage boundary.

search-host-restrict|C|C4|crest|Why use a site restriction when searching public documents?|Reduce unrelated indexed results to the chosen site scope|Force the server to reveal private files|Authenticate as a website administrator|Perform a DNS zone transfer through the browser|Search restrictions improve collection relevance; they operate on indexed data, not direct filesystem permissions.|Search syntax selects results rather than granting access.

filetype-content|C|C4|crest|Why inspect a retrieved document rather than trusting only its .pdf filename?|Names and extensions do not establish actual content or relevance|Every extension is a signed content guarantee|Only PDFs can disclose sensitive information|A .pdf suffix grants extraction rights automatically|Content, metadata, source, and date determine usefulness. File naming alone can be misleading.|A filename is one clue among several.

search-cache-limit|C|C4|crest|A search snippet contains text that the current page lacks. What should be considered?|Index timing, alternate views, and snippet generation|That the current server must have been compromised|That the snippet proves a live credential|That the browser has administrator privileges|Search engines maintain their own representations of content. Correlate the source and retrieval times.|Indexed presentation can lag live content.

mailing-list-version|C|C5|nntp|A staff post says the company used version X two years ago. How should it be used?|As historical technical context requiring current corroboration|As proof that every current host still runs X|As a valid password for every employee|As permission to attack the author's home machine|Public discussions may reveal useful technology and migration history. Current deployment claims require more evidence.|Historical firsthand statements can still become stale.

mailing-list-identity|C|C5|nntp|A public mailing-list author uses an address at the target domain. What does it initially support?|A possible organizational association|A guaranteed privileged domain account|A guarantee the author controls every server|A universal authorization from the organization|An address can be a clue but may be an alias, reused identity, or historical association.|Public affiliation is not verified account privilege.

nntp-group|C|C5|nntp|What does selecting an NNTP newsgroup primarily establish?|The article context for subsequent group-oriented operations|Administrator control of the news server|A DNS delegation to the group name|A private shell on the article author's computer|NNTP groups organize articles. Selection and reading permissions are separate server behavior.|A group identifier is a content namespace.

nntp-message-id|C|C5|nntp|Why is a news article's Message-ID useful for evidence correlation?|It can identify a particular article across references or copies|It is the author's password hash|It proves the contents are cryptographically signed|It lists every machine on the author's network|Identifiers support correlation, subject to format and provenance. They are not secret account credentials.|An identifier and an authenticator are different artifacts.

nntp-crosspost|C|C5|nntp|The same article appears in several newsgroups. How should evidence be interpreted?|It may be one cross-posted source, not independent confirmations|Each appearance proves a separate organization's endorsement|Each copy grants additional test scope|Cross-posting changes the author's OS privilege|Recognize shared origin when weighing evidence. Multiple copies do not necessarily increase independence.|Repeated publication is not independent corroboration.

nntp-transport|C|C5|nntp|Which conventional port pair is associated with NNTP and implicit-TLS news access?|TCP/119 and TCP/563|UDP/119 and UDP/563|TCP/110 and TCP/995|TCP/143 and TCP/993|These are common news-access conventions. STARTTLS, deployment settings, and actual protocol responses need separate checks.|Specify protocol, transport, and protection mode.

archive-attribution|C|C5|nntp|A mirrored discussion archive strips some headers. What should its analysis preserve?|The mirror provenance and missing original metadata|A claim that the mirror authenticates every author|A claim that all timestamps are necessarily exact|Only the archive's visual theme|Mirrors can alter presentation or omit context. Attribute observations to the actual retained source.|A convenient copy may not preserve every provenance field.

news-sensitive|C|C5|nntp|A public troubleshooting post includes an internal hostname and path. What is its likely reconnaissance value?|Architecture and naming clues for later corroboration|Automatic remote access to that host|A guarantee the path is public on the website|An authenticated administrator session|Posts can leak structure without exposing a direct access path. Preserve what was actually disclosed.|Information can be valuable without being a working exploit.

received-order|C|C6|headers|Why read Received trace fields with their insertion order in mind?|Servers typically prepend their own trace information|Each server overwrites every previous field|The lowest field is always cryptographically trusted|The order is determined by the sender's DNS TTL|Trace order supports route interpretation, while the trusted boundary determines which claims can be relied on.|Order and trust are separate interpretive requirements.

from-envelope|C|C6|smtp|Why distinguish a visible From header from the SMTP envelope sender?|They are separate fields with different routing and display roles|Both must always have identical values|From is the server's TLS certificate name|The envelope sender is the recipient's password|A message's presented author and transport envelope can differ. Authentication policy provides further context.|Displayed identity is not the entire transport identity.

reply-to|C|C6|headers|What does Reply-To conventionally influence?|Where a mail client directs a reply|Which account controls the SMTP server|The sender's verified employee role|The server's listening TCP port|Reply-To is message metadata, not authentication proof. Differences from From can be meaningful but not conclusive by themselves.|A response address need not be the verified original sender.

return-path|C|C6|smtp|What does Return-Path commonly record after delivery?|The transport envelope's reverse-path address|Every message recipient's private key|The domain's administrator password|The browser session that composed the message|The reverse path relates to delivery/error handling. It is distinct from display headers and does not establish a human's identity.|A transport address has a specific protocol role.

messageid-domain|C|C6|headers|A Message-ID includes an internal-looking domain. What can it support?|A naming or generating-system lead|Proof that the named host is publicly reachable|Proof of a particular user's password|Permission to scan every suffix-related domain|Message generation conventions can disclose clues, but fields can be configured or forged. Correlate with trusted evidence.|A header string is not an authenticated topology map.

x-mailer|C|C6|headers|An X-Mailer field names a product version. How should this be treated?|A sender-supplied fingerprint to corroborate|A signed guarantee of every server patch|An authorization token for the mailbox|A complete description of the delivery path|Client identifiers may be absent, modified, or spoofed. They can guide hypotheses without proving current applicability.|A claimed client version is not a verified software inventory.

internal-ip-header|C|C6|headers|A trusted relay adds a private address in a trace field. What is disclosed?|A potentially internal hop or endpoint clue|A public route to every private subnet|Every account's exact Windows SID|A guaranteed remotely exploitable service|The field may reveal addressing context. Reachability, owner, service, and current state need separate assessment.|Topology clues do not establish a network path.

auth-results|C|C6|headers|Why consider who inserted an Authentication-Results header?|A sender can forge an apparent result outside the trusted boundary|Every such header is signed by the recipient automatically|Its name guarantees its content is authoritative|It replaces all message-source interpretation|Trust results produced by the relevant receiving infrastructure, not arbitrary copied or injected fields.|Security metadata must itself have trusted provenance.

dkim-body|C|C6|headers|A message has a valid DKIM result from a trusted verifier. What should not be inferred automatically?|That the human author is who the recipient assumes|Integrity of the signed portions under that signing domain|An association with the signing domain's key|That signature verification succeeded for the assessed content|Domain-level signing and human identity are different claims. Scope, signing coverage, and policy still matter.|A domain signature is not complete person authentication.

collection-correlation|C|C6|crest|A hostname appears in DNS, a certificate log, and an old email. What improves attribution confidence?|Independent current corroboration with source/time context|Counting copied records as separate proof|Discarding every conflicting timestamp|Assuming the oldest mention proves current ownership|Several sources can strengthen a hypothesis if genuinely independent and relevant. Resolve history and discrepancies explicitly.|Evidence quantity and evidence independence differ.

passive-target-content|C|C3|crest|Why is directly fetching a target website generally active collection relative to that server?|It sends a request to the target service|Only POST can contact a server|GET requests are never logged|Public accessibility makes all requests passive|A read operation can still generate contact and logs. Passive often refers to collecting through other sources without direct target interaction.|Read-only and passive are not synonyms.

recon-threat-link|C|C3|crest|An exposed API schema names an export operation. What is a useful next analysis step?|Identify its inputs, identity requirements, and data boundary|Assume it exports every record anonymously|Ignore it because no HTML button exists|Treat the schema as a grant of administrator access|Discovery should inform a testable model of functionality and trust. Actual endpoint behavior supplies stronger evidence.|A schema is a map to investigate, not an exploitation result.

search-hit-current|C|C1|wstg|A search engine shows an old admin page URL. What does that establish without a fresh check?|A historical indexing lead|A currently reachable authentication bypass|The administrator's present password|An exact current software patch level|Search results can be stale or reflect past content. Verify current reachability and behavior within scope.|An indexed record is not a current service observation.
